title: 1 Kings 11:1–13
context: 1 Kings 11 describes the decline of Solomon’s reign. His many foreign marriages, some perhaps political alliances, turn his heart in old age after the gods of surrounding nations, and he builds shrines to them near Jerusalem. The LORD, who had appeared to him twice, is angry and announces that he will tear the kingdom from Solomon’s son, leaving one tribe for David’s and Jerusalem’s sake. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground about judgment on idolatry and God’s faithfulness to David.

verses.text: Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh: women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites,
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon loves many foreign women, including Pharaoh’s daughter and women from Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon, and the Hittites. The concern the narrator raises is religious, not ethnic.

Arminian readers see a king making choices that will draw his heart away from God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list names peoples associated with other gods. Deuteronomy 17:17 had warned that a king’s many wives would turn his heart away.

Reformed readers see the warning coming true. Both traditions read this soberly as shared ground about the danger of divided loyalty.

verses.text: of the nations concerning which the LORD said to the children of Israel, “You shall not go among them, neither shall they come among you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods.” Solomon joined to these in love.
verses.arminianNotes:
These are nations about which the LORD had warned that they would turn Israel’s heart after their gods, yet Solomon ‘joined to these in love.’ He knowingly crosses a boundary.

Arminian readers see clear warning disregarded by free choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator quotes the earlier command (compare Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3–4). The issue is worship, not marriage as such.

Reformed readers see the heart’s attachments shaping its worship. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the prohibition guarded Israel’s exclusive loyalty to the LORD.

verses.text: He had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines. His wives turned his heart away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon has seven hundred wives of royal rank and three hundred concubines, and his wives turn his heart away. The numbers are stated without elaboration.

Arminian readers see accumulation and alliance replacing wholehearted devotion. The point is where his heart goes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Some of these marriages may have served political alliances (compare 3:1), though the text focuses on their spiritual effect.

Reformed readers see excess leading to idolatry. Both traditions read the verse soberly and as shared ground, centering on the turning of Solomon’s heart rather than on the household itself.

verses.text: When Solomon was old, his wives turned away his heart after other gods; and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father was.
verses.arminianNotes:
In his old age, Solomon’s wives turn his heart after other gods, and his heart is not fully true to the LORD as David’s was. The decline is gradual.

Arminian readers see that early faithfulness does not guarantee later faithfulness. Choices accumulate.
verses.reformedNotes:
The comparison with David concerns loyalty in worship; David sinned gravely but did not turn to other gods.

Reformed readers see the need for ongoing grace and watchfulness. Both traditions read this as shared ground and as a sober warning to finish faithfully.

verses.text: For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon follows Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Milcom of the Ammonites. The narrator names the gods plainly.

Arminian readers see real apostasy by a king who had known the LORD intimately. His wisdom did not protect him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Milcom is called ‘the abomination of the Ammonites.’ The language expresses the narrator’s judgment.

Reformed readers see how far a gifted servant can fall. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of idolatry, which Nehemiah 13:26 later recalls as a warning.

verses.text: Solomon did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and didn’t go fully after the LORD, as David his father did.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon does evil in the LORD’s sight and does not fully follow the LORD as David did. The verdict is clear.

Arminian readers see personal responsibility for a divided heart. The narrator holds Solomon accountable.
verses.reformedNotes:
‘Didn’t go fully after the LORD’ names partial devotion. The phrase contrasts with Caleb, who ‘wholly followed’ the LORD (Joshua 14:8).

Reformed readers see half-hearted worship as itself a form of unfaithfulness. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about wholehearted loyalty to God.

verses.text: Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, on the mountain that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech the abomination of the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon builds high places for Chemosh of Moab and Molech of Ammon on the mountain before Jerusalem. Idolatry becomes public and visible.

Arminian readers see private compromise turning into public example.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shrines stand within sight of the temple Solomon built. 2 Kings 23:13 later records Josiah defiling them.

Reformed readers see the contradiction of a temple-builder sponsoring idols. Both traditions read this as shared ground; the exact location of the mountain is commonly linked with the Mount of Olives, though the text does not name it.

verses.text: So he did for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
He does this for all his foreign wives, who burn incense and sacrifice to their gods. The worship is widespread.

Arminian readers see accommodation becoming a policy rather than a lapse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Solomon provides for the worship of every wife’s gods. The scale of the compromise is emphasized.

Reformed readers see how one compromise multiplies into many. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the narrator’s concern with the influence a king’s choices have on the worship of the whole nation.

verses.text: The LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD is angry with Solomon because his heart turned away from the God who appeared to him twice. Privilege increases responsibility.

Arminian readers see God’s anger as a just response to a real betrayal of a real relationship.
verses.reformedNotes:
The two appearances were at Gibeon (3:5) and after the temple’s dedication (9:2). Solomon had received great grace.

Reformed readers see the seriousness of sinning against such favor. Both traditions read God’s anger as shared ground about judgment on idolatry.

verses.text: and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods; but he didn’t keep that which the LORD commanded.
verses.arminianNotes:
God had commanded Solomon not to go after other gods, but he did not keep the command. The warning of 9:6–7 had been explicit.

Arminian readers see disobedience in the face of clear knowledge.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator stresses that Solomon was warned specifically. His failure was not ignorance.

Reformed readers see the persistence of sin even in the wise and favored. Both traditions read this as shared ground, emphasizing that God’s commands were plain and his judgment is just.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, “Because this is done by you, and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes, which I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you, and will give it to your servant.
verses.arminianNotes:
God tells Solomon he will tear the kingdom from him and give it to his servant, because he has not kept the covenant. Judgment is announced.

Arminian readers see the covenant’s conditions taken seriously by God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The kingdom will be torn away, as Saul’s was (1 Samuel 15:28). The language of tearing recurs.

Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness and covenant judgment together. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s just response to idolatry, without inventing a dispute about salvation.

verses.text: Nevertheless, I will not do it in your days, for David your father’s sake; but I will tear it out of your son’s hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will not do it in Solomon’s days, for David’s sake, but will tear it from his son. Judgment is delayed.

Arminian readers see mercy tempering judgment because of God’s promise to David.
verses.reformedNotes:
The delay is ‘for David your father’s sake.’ God honors his covenant with David (2 Samuel 7).

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his promises even amid judgment. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s mercy and fidelity.

verses.text: However, I will not tear away all the kingdom; but I will give one tribe to your son, for David my servant’s sake, and for Jerusalem’s sake which I have chosen.”
verses.arminianNotes:
God will not tear away the whole kingdom but will leave one tribe to Solomon’s son, for David’s and Jerusalem’s sake. A remnant remains.

Arminian readers see God preserving his purpose through a faithful line despite failure.
verses.reformedNotes:
One tribe is kept for David and for the chosen city. Interpreters explain the tribal arithmetic in different ways.

Reformed readers see God’s covenant purposes standing firm. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the Davidic line preserved for the promises still to come.
